opus-5.5.text:
I think it depends a bit on what you mean by continual learning, because the term gets used pretty loosely. In the strict academic sense, continual learning means a system that keeps updating itself on a stream of new data without catastrophically forgetting what it already knew, and ideally without someone stepping in to retrain it from scratch. By that definition, most deployed robot systems today aren't really doing it yet.

What we usually see in practice is a loop. You deploy a policy, the robots collect experience, some of it successes and a lot of it failures or interventions, and that data goes back into a central pool. Then at some point you retrain or fine-tune and push a new model out. That's very valuable, and arguably it's the most practical way to get improvement from deployment right now, but I'd call it iterated offline learning rather than true continual learning. The learning happens in discrete batches, and humans are still deciding when to retrain, what data to include, and whether the new model is good enough to ship.

The way I'd assess whether something really counts comes down to a few questions. First, does the system improve on the specific task or environment it's in while it's operating, or only after a round trip through a training pipeline? Second, does it hold on to its general capabilities as it specializes, or does it get better at folding towels in one particular home and worse at everything else? Third, how much human curation is in the loop? If someone has to label every episode or hand-pick the data, that's closer to a data collection strategy than a self-improving system.

I think we're moving toward the real thing. With large pretrained models you have a strong prior, so a small amount of on-the-job experience can go a long way, and you can start thinking about things like reinforcement learning from the robot's own rollouts, or learned reward models that judge success without a human checking. But I'd be honest that it's still an open problem. Doing that safely and stably on physical hardware, where mistakes cost something and the data distribution keeps shifting, is hard. So my answer is that deployment-time learning is a necessary ingredient, but it only becomes continual learning when the updates are ongoing, largely autonomous, and don't erode what the robot could already do.

r001.rationale: The response assesses continual learning through gradations in deployment-time improvement, autonomy, and human curation, distinguishing batch retraining from ongoing on-the-job updates rather than treating it as a simple yes-or-no label.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it depends on what you're actually asking the system to do, and most of the time the word "continual learning" gets used more loosely than it should.

If a robot is deployed and you're collecting data from it, shipping that back to a datacenter, retraining a policy, and redeploying, I'd call that iterative data collection and fine-tuning. It's useful, it's how a lot of real systems work, but there's a human in the loop deciding when to retrain, and the model itself isn't really changing in response to what it experiences in the moment.

What I'd want to see before I'd call it continual learning is a few things. First, the learning has to be happening more or less on the robot's timescale, not on the release cycle. The system encounters something it hasn't seen, and that experience changes its behavior soon after, without someone curating a dataset and kicking off a job. Second, it has to be cumulative. It can't just adapt to the current task and lose what it knew about previous ones, which is the classic forgetting problem, and that's still genuinely hard. And third, and this is the one people skip, it should be improving in some measurable sense across tasks, not just drifting. Adaptation that makes the robot worse at the thing it was doing last week isn't learning, it's degradation.

The test I like is pretty simple. Take the same robot at month one and month six, give it the task it was originally trained on and a task it only encountered in deployment, and look at both. If the deployment-only task is better and the original task hasn't gotten worse, and nobody retrained it offline in between, that's continual learning. If you can't say yes to all three of those, you probably have something else, and it's fine to have something else, but we should be clear about what it is.

The other part that matters to me is the data side. When a robot learns from its own experience, a lot of that experience is from its own, often suboptimal, behavior. So the real question is whether you can turn that into a useful signal without a human labeling it, whether that's through reward models, through self-supervised objectives on the sensor stream, or through some notion of success you can detect automatically. If the robot still needs a person to tell it what went well, then it's learning from the person, not from experience.

r001.rationale: The response gives criteria and an all-or-nothing test for calling a system continual learning; it does not frame the concept as a spectrum based on how much the robot learns on the job.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by continual learning. If you deploy a robot, collect experience, and use that experience to improve its policy, then in a broad sense, yes, that’s continual learning. But that alone doesn’t tell you whether you’ve solved the interesting problems associated with it.

For me, the questions are: Can the robot acquire new skills while retaining the ones it already has? Can it adapt as its environment changes? And can it do that with a reasonable amount of data and computation, without us having to intervene every time?

You might collect data from deployed robots and periodically retrain a model on all the accumulated experience. That can be a very useful system, but I’d distinguish it from a robot that learns incrementally from its own experience under limited memory and compute. So I’d look less at whether it qualifies for the label and more at what actually improves over time, what it forgets, and how much machinery is needed to keep that learning going.

r001.rationale: The response treats the label as dependent on the degree and kind of learning: it distinguishes broad post-deployment retraining from incremental learning and focuses on what improves over time and what the robot can retain or adapt to, rather than making the label a simple yes-or-no test.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by continual learning. If a robot is deployed, collects experience, and we use that experience to update its policy, then in a broad sense, yes, that is continual learning. The learning process hasn’t stopped at deployment.

But there’s a stronger version of the question: can it learn something new while retaining the things it could already do? Can it adapt as its environment changes, over a long period of time, without us repeatedly resetting the training process or carefully curating all the data? That’s a much more demanding criterion.

So I would look at the actual setup. What changes over time? What does the robot get to retain and replay? How much human intervention is involved? And are we measuring performance on earlier skills as well as the latest thing it learned? Just showing that a robot improves with more experience doesn’t, by itself, establish that it has solved those harder continual-learning problems.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes broad continual learning from a stronger, more demanding version and evaluates the robot’s learning setup and capabilities. This frames continual learning as having degrees rather than a simple yes-or-no classification.
